articles.summary: Japan, South Korea Stocks Rebound as Chips Rally  Markets.com
articles.full_text:
Japanese and South Korean stocks rebounded in early trading on Wednesday, October 21, with semiconductor leaders helping lift both markets as investors assessed overnight U.S. earnings developments.
South Korea’s KOSPI opened 2.05% higher at 5,666.34. Japan’s Nikkei 225 opened up 1.26% at 64,885.95 before extending its advance to 1.41%, reaching 64,979.50.
The recovery gathered pace in Seoul. By 9:30 a.m. Korea Standard Time, the KOSPI had climbed 3.62% to 5,753.55, showing that buying continued beyond the opening jump.
The distinction matters for readers following the session: the initial 2.05% increase represented the KOSPI’s opening move, while subsequent reports captured a stronger intraday recovery. Neither figure represented the closing result.
The early gains suggested renewed appetite for technology exposure. However, the performance of a single morning session provides limited evidence about whether the recent pressure on the sector has ended.
South Korean memory manufacturers were among the main beneficiaries of the recovery.
Samsung Electronics initially gained 2.72%, while SK Hynix advanced 3.92%. Both extended their gains as the morning progressed, rising approximately 6% and 7%, respectively, by 9:30 a.m. local time.
In Japan, Kioxia climbed 5.18% in early trading, while SoftBank Group rose 3.56%.
The simultaneous advances placed memory and AI-related companies at the centre of the regional rebound. Their performance also made sector breadth an important consideration: sustained gains across more companies would provide stronger evidence of improving sentiment than a rally concentrated in a few large names.
For market participants, the immediate question is whether buying can persist through the session and into subsequent trading days. Strong opening moves can reflect improving expectations, but they can also lose momentum as investors reassess valuations and upcoming results.
Fresh figures from Super Micro Computer provided a more concrete development for investors assessing AI infrastructure demand.
The company estimated revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion for its fiscal first quarter ended September 30, above its previous guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. It attributed the increase primarily to stronger demand for AI platforms.
Supermicro also estimated gross margins of 12.0% to 12.5%, compared with earlier guidance of 10.4% to 10.8%, citing customer and product mix.
The update offered evidence that demand could translate into both higher sales and better margins at an AI server supplier. That combination may support sentiment toward the wider infrastructure supply chain.
However, the figures remain preliminary and unaudited. Supermicro said its final results could differ as it completes its financial closing procedures.
The update also cannot establish the earnings outlook for every semiconductor company. Individual suppliers face different product mixes, customer relationships and production costs.
U.S. extended-hours trading showed that investors continued to distinguish sharply between corporate results.
SpaceX shares rose more than 8% later in the after-hours session following stronger-than-expected quarterly results. Supermicro also rallied sharply after its preliminary business update.
Netflix moved in the opposite direction, falling approximately 6% after its earnings release.
The streaming company reported quarterly earnings of $0.87 per share, above the $0.82 consensus estimate, while revenue of $12.87 billion matched expectations. Nevertheless, a reduction in its advertising revenue outlook raised concerns about future growth.
The contrasting reactions illustrated why an earnings beat alone may provide limited support for a share price. Investors also assess guidance, the durability of revenue growth and how much optimism is already reflected in valuations.
For Asian technology shares, the positive AI-related updates offered a supportive backdrop. Netflix’s decline nevertheless showed that company-specific disappointments could still generate substantial selling.
The Asian rebound followed a mixed U.S. regular session on Tuesday, October 20.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to close at 52,495.88. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to 7,712.57, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.02% to 26,424.82.
Strong corporate earnings supported the broader market, while a retreat in oil prices helped equities recover from earlier weakness. However, declines in several large technology companies limited the Nasdaq’s performance.
That divergence matters when interpreting Wednesday’s Asian gains. The overnight session offered support from broader equities, but U.S. technology stocks had yet to demonstrate a uniform recovery during regular trading.
Subsequent after-hours advances therefore represented a further shift in sentiment, rather than a continuation of an across-the-board technology rally.
Attention now turns to additional corporate results, including Tesla and Meta Platforms, and what their updates reveal about spending, profitability and growth expectations.
For semiconductor investors, the central issue remains whether investment in AI infrastructure can produce sustainable revenue and earnings across the supply chain. Strong demand announcements help, but margins and financial returns remain equally relevant.
The breadth of the Asian rebound will also matter. Continued participation beyond Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and a small group of Japanese technology names could strengthen the recovery. A narrow advance would leave index performance more dependent on a handful of stocks.
Japan and South Korea’s early gains marked an improvement in technology sentiment, supported by rising semiconductor shares and encouraging U.S. corporate updates. Whether that recovery lasts will depend on subsequent earnings, buying beyond the opening session and further evidence that AI demand can support profitable growth.

articles.title: Japan says rare earth yttrium supplies have stalled amid China export controls - Malay Mail
articles.summary: Japan says rare earth yttrium supplies have stalled amid China export controls  Malay Mail
articles.full_text:
TOKYO, Oct 21 — Global exports of the rare earth yttrium have stalled, causing what a Japanese official described as a “supply-demand crunch”, with the Financial Times reporting that Tokyo was months away from running out of the critical metal.
Yttrium is essential for manufacturing consumer electronics, LEDs, aviation engines, semiconductor production equipment and a variety of industrial products.
China accounts for almost two-thirds of rare earth mining production and 92 per cent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency.
“It is true that exports of yttrium have stalled not only to Japan but worldwide, causing a supply-demand crunch and soaring prices,” a Japanese industry ministry official told AFP today, on condition of anonymity.
“Exports to Japan have decreased, including delays in shipments, and the global volume itself is low,” the official said.
The comments came after the Financial Times reported that Japan could exhaust its supply of the critical material in “months”.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in July that yttrium was “globally scarce” and was “an important rare earth for our country”.
According to Chinese customs data, exports of yttrium oxide to Japan amounted to 4,000 kilograms in September, compared with 51,000 kilograms in the same period the previous year.
The industry ministry official said Tokyo was working with the United States and European nations on critical mineral resources and rare earths, including yttrium.
Beijing has intensified pressure on Tokyo since Takaichi hinted last November that Japan could intervene militarily in any attack on self-ruled Taiwan.
China views Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out taking it by force.
“China imposed export controls on Japan in accordance with laws and regulations, with the aim of curbing Japan’s attempts at remilitarisation and possessing nuclear weapons,” Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing today.
Japan has asked the US government and American businesses to press China to ease rare earth export controls to avoid “severe disruption to the global automotive, defence and chip industries”, the Financial Times report said.
US defence supply chains rely on Japanese components that use yttrium, the newspaper said. — AFP

articles.title: Lee Kun-hee's 1974 Investment Launched South Korea's Semiconductor Empire - 조선일보
articles.summary: Lee Kun-hee's 1974 Investment Launched South Korea's Semiconductor Empire  조선일보
articles.full_text:
The 19th Semiconductor Day commemorative ceremony was held on the 21st. Semiconductor Day was established to mark October 29, 1994, when South Korea’s annual semiconductor exports first surpassed 10 billion dollars. Thirty-two years later, this year, South Korea’s semiconductor exports exceeded 340 billion dollars as of September. The 10 billion dollars in exports from 1994 now equates to just ten days’ worth of semiconductor exports today. The starting point of South Korea’s now-giant semiconductor industry was a personal investment of 500,000 dollars thrown into a venture company on the brink of bankruptcy. It was the late Lee Kun-hee, Samsung chairman, who injected 500,000 dollars of his personal funds to acquire a 50% stake in Hankook Semiconductor in December 1974, six years before his passing on the 25th, which marks the sixth anniversary of his death this year.
Established in early 1974, Hankook Semiconductor was South Korea’s first private wafer-processing company. However, it faced bankruptcy within less than a year. Lee Kun-hee, then 32 years old and a director at Tongyang Broadcasting (TBC), used his personal funds to acquire the stake. Opposition within Samsung was strong, with critics arguing, “Pursuing high-tech industries is reckless when we can’t even make TVs properly.” But he later reflected, “During the oil shock, I realized that a country without natural resources could only survive through high-tech industries created by the mind.” That Hankook Semiconductor became the foundation of Samsung Electronics’ current semiconductor (DS) division.
There was no original technology. Overseas consulting firms and U.S. and Japanese semiconductor companies recommended starting with non-memory chips for home appliances or simple assembly and processing, which required less initial capital. However, Lee Kun-hee insisted on a “direct push into memory chips,” betting on lowering costs through large-scale equipment investments to compete in the global market. To persuade his father, Lee Byung-chul, the founder, who favored a cautious approach of testing every step, he frequently compiled and submitted data. He also invited Japanese engineers to South Korea every weekend to acquire technology. As a result, on February 1983, Lee Byung-chul officially declared Samsung’s entry into semiconductors in Tokyo—eight years after acquiring Hankook Semiconductor’s stake. In December that year, Samsung became the third company in the world, after the U.S. and Japan, to successfully develop a 64K DRAM. However, losses continued, with the company losing 1 dollar per chip sold.
During the development of the 4-megabit DRAM in 1987, a debate erupted between the “stack method” of layering circuits upward and the “trench method” of etching substrates downward—neither of which U.S. or Japanese companies had solved. Lee Kun-hee, then vice chairman, decisively ended the debate by stating, “We go with the stack method.” He judged that the simpler structure would be advantageous for mass production and defect correction. While Japan’s top company, Toshiba, which chose the trench method, struggled with mass production yield issues, Samsung, which maximized productivity with the stack method, dominated the DRAM market. Lee later said, “I had a hunch the stack method was right, but I wasn’t 100% sure. We were lucky.”
The decisive blow to widen the gap was preemptive investments even during downturns. In 1993, he introduced an 8-inch wafer line, which had double the production capacity of the then-standard 6-inch wafers, when competitors hesitated due to technical burdens. This investment allowed Samsung to rank first in global memory semiconductor sales in October that year. Even when DRAM prices plummeted due to the dot-com bubble collapse in 2000, he pushed for the world’s first transition to 12-inch wafers. His urging of the hesitant Samsung management to “hurry up” and invest paid off.

articles.title: South Korea Dominates HBM for AI Chips - 조선일보
articles.summary: South Korea Dominates HBM for AI Chips  조선일보
articles.full_text:
In the race to lead in artificial intelligence (AI), the demand for superior AI processing chips and more memory semiconductors has intensified the global semiconductor industry’s endless competition over manufacturing technologies.
The most intense battleground lies in memory semiconductors, particularly HBM (high-bandwidth memory) used in AI accelerators like those from NVIDIA. The most advanced product is the 6th-generation HBM4, which only three companies—Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and U.S.-based Micron—can produce.
Chinese memory firms still struggle to produce HBM effectively. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix held a 50% market share in HBM in the second quarter of this year, followed by Samsung Electronics at 33%. Micron ranked third with 18%. The industry estimates that Chinese HBM technology lags South Korea by over three years.
In contrast, Chinese firms are gaining ground in the general DRAM and NAND flash markets. In the second-quarter global DRAM market, Chinese ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) claimed a 10% share, ranking fourth behind Samsung Electronics (38%), SK Hynix (25%), and Micron (24%).
While South Korean products still lead technologically, the AI boom-driven DRAM shortage has opened opportunities for CXMT. South Korean semiconductor companies’ most advanced DRAM is the 1c process (early 10-nanometer class, with 1 nanometer equaling one-billionth of a meter). Comparing Samsung’s 1983-developed 64Kb DRAM to today’s 1c-process 24Gb DRAM used in HBM4, chip capacity has grown approximately 390,000 times, while circuit line widths have shrunk to a fraction of their original size. Meanwhile, CXMT’s recently mass-produced process technology is five years behind Samsung’s. However, CXMT has announced plans to adopt the 4F² design technology—reducing DRAM cell area—within the year, effectively declaring its intent to overtake Samsung and SK Hynix.
In NAND flash, Chinese Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation (YMTC) is rapidly closing the gap. In the second-quarter shipment rankings, YMTC held a 16.5% share, placing third behind Samsung and SK Hynix. Its technological prowess is notable: leveraging its proprietary “Xtacking” stacking technology, YMTC is developing products exceeding 300 layers. The industry consensus is that South Korea and China now have virtually no technological gap in NAND flash.
The non-memory (system semiconductor) sector is dominated by the U.S. and Taiwan. The CPU market is split between U.S. firms Intel and AMD, while NVIDIA commands over 80% of the GPU market. Though Chinese companies like Huawei have developed their own GPUs and AI chips, their performance lags behind U.S. counterparts.
In foundry (semiconductor contract manufacturing), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) leads with a 72.5% global market share in the second quarter, according to TrendForce. Samsung Electronics ranked second with 5.9%, followed by China’s Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) at 5.4%. Both TSMC and Samsung have entered the 2-nanometer process, but TSMC is reported to have a significant lead in yield rates.

articles.title: South Korea's AI Trade Roars Back: Samsung and SK Hynix Lead $160 Billion Market Rebound - Benzinga
articles.summary: South Korea's AI Trade Roars Back: Samsung and SK Hynix Lead $160 Billion Market Rebound  Benzinga
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose as much as 5% on Wednesday, prompting the Korea Exchange to initiate a temporary restriction on program buying. The increase reversed a market decline from the previous day and was driven by investors purchasing shares of semiconductor manufacturers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
Tech Gains Drive Market Rebound
The Korea Exchange suspended program buying for five minutes when the Kospi index experienced a 4.7% surge, according to a post by the X account Bull Theory. This market movement added over 238 trillion won, or 160 billion dollars, to the value of South Korean equities.
At the last check during the trading session, shares of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix increased by up to 4.84% and 4.09%, respectively. This rebound follows a volatile period for South Korean stocks; the Kospi index more than doubled in the first half of the year before experiencing multiple downturns, including a nearly 40% drop from its peak in June.
Elice Recovers Following IPO Decline
The broader market recovery aligned with a reversal for Kosdaq-listed Elice, an artificial intelligence cloud and data center operator. After falling 32% during its initial trading day on Tuesday, Elice shares surged 29.92% to 79,900 won, hitting the daily upper limit on Wednesday, after plunging 32% on their debut a day earlier. The shares remained about 11.7% below their 90,500-won IPO price.
According to a Business Insider report, Elice Chief Executive Officer Jae Won Kim addressed the market fluctuations, saying, “I’m not worried about the volatility issues in the first week.”
Kim also noted that Elice expects its revenue to at least double this year. According to its IPO prospectus, Elice reported first-half revenue of 34.4 billion won, roughly $26 million, triple the year-earlier level, along with operating profit of 10.3 billion won.
Wall Street and Asian Markets
The South Korean rally followed a mixed overnight session on Wall Street, where the Dow climbed 1.02% and the S&P 500 rose 0.28%, while the Nasdaq declined slightly amid ongoing concerns regarding AI spending.
Across broader Asian markets, performance was mixed; the Taiwan index gained 1.01%, and the Nikkei rose 0.86%, while the Shanghai and Shenzhen indexes both recorded declines of 0.31%.

articles.title: South Korea Overtakes Japan in Global Export Rankings - 조선일보
articles.summary: South Korea Overtakes Japan in Global Export Rankings  조선일보
articles.full_text:
The AI (artificial intelligence)-driven semiconductor super cycle has completely reshaped the global trade landscape in just one year. According to an analysis by Chosun Ilbo and KOTRA, Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency, of World Trade Organization (WTO) and major countries’ statistics on the 21st, the owners of six positions from 5th to 10th among the world’s top 10 exporters in the first half of this year have changed. This is the most turbulent shift since 2009, when China overtook Germany to claim the top spot during the global financial crisis.
At the eye of the typhoon is South Korea, the world’s leading memory powerhouse. South Korea is on the verge of achieving its first-ever exports of 1 trillion dollars (semiconductors are projected to reach 400 billion dollars) this year. With its first-half exports (496.1 billion dollars) surging 48.2% compared to the same period last year, it jumped from 7th place last year to 5th. Not only did it overtake Japan, long considered an insurmountable rival, but it also closed in on the Netherlands (531.5 billion dollars), a global intermediary trade powerhouse and a member of the top four.
Korean memory chips have propelled trading partners’ rankings through global supply chains. Taiwan, which imports Korean HBM (high-bandwidth memory) to assemble AI accelerators, rose from 11th to 6th. Mexico, which assembles servers for the U.S. using Asian semiconductor components, climbed from 10th to 8th. Singapore, a semiconductor back-end and intermediary hub, entered the top 10 from 13th. Meanwhile, traditional manufacturing powerhouse Japan fell from 5th to 9th, while 3rd-place Germany stagnated. Semiconductors are reshaping global trade power.
◇Powered by the Semiconductor Engine… South Korea’s Exports Surge 48%, Taiwan’s 46% in First Half
South Korea’s semiconductor exports surpassed 60 billion dollars in a single month for the first time last month. This is nearly equivalent to Japan’s average monthly total exports (64.7 billion dollars) this year. A single product—semiconductors—now matches Japan’s entire export volume. Currently, an average of 4.74 billion dollars worth of “Made in Korea” goods are shipped worldwide every day, exceeding 50,000 dollars per second.
Explosive semiconductor exports are altering the global trade map. Until last year, Japan was the world’s 5th-largest exporter, behind only China, the U.S., Germany, and the Netherlands, with Italy ahead of 7th-place South Korea. However, within a year, the “semiconductor gold rush” triggered by global Big Tech’s AI (artificial intelligence) data center expansion has propelled South Korea and other AI supply chain nations upward, while traditional manufacturing powers reliant on automobiles and chemicals have fallen behind.
① Beyond Overtaking Japan for the First Time, South Korea Eyes the Netherlands’ Top Four Status
In 2005, South Korea’s exports (284.4 billion dollars) were less than half (48%) of Japan’s (595.3 billion dollars). Twenty-one years later, in 2026, South Korea has finally distanced itself from Japan by a wide margin. From January to August this year, South Korea’s exports reached 693.6 billion dollars, surpassing Japan’s 517.4 billion dollars by 176.2 billion dollars. South Korea’s export growth rate (52.9%) during this period was nearly three times that of China (18.3%) and seven times Japan’s (7.7%). Semiconductors accounted for 74% of the increase.
South Korea’s semiconductor exports from January to August surged 171.7% year-on-year to 280 billion dollars, a net increase of 176.9 billion dollars from last year. In contrast, Japan’s automotive exports—a key sector—grew by only 2.2% (78.1 billion dollars), a mere 1.7 billion dollar increase. South Korea’s semiconductor export growth rate was over 100 times that of Japan’s automotive sector.
South Korea is now threatening 4th-place Netherlands. The gap with the Netherlands, based on first-half figures, is only 35.4 billion dollars. South Korea is poised to surpass the European intermediary trade hub, which fills half of its exports through re-exports, purely through manufacturing strength. At the current pace, entering the “world’s top four” is no longer a distant dream, analysts say.
② The Butterfly Effect of K-Memory… Taiwan, Mexico, and Singapore Leap Forward
Korean memory chips have lifted trading partners’ export rankings through global division of labor. Taiwan, a foundry powerhouse that exclusively outsources GPU production, saw its exports jump 46.1% in the first half, rising five spots from 11th to 6th. AI accelerators assembled by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and exported to U.S. Big Tech include Korean HBM. This explains why South Korea’s exports to Taiwan surged 61.3% to 47.5 billion dollars from January to August.
The ripple effect extended to Mexico and Southeast Asia. Mexico, which rose to 8th place in global exports, has transformed into an AI server assembly base targeting the North American market. From January to August, South Korea’s semiconductor exports to Mexico exploded by 293.4%, and computer component exports surged 725.0%. Singapore, which entered the top 10 for the first time, also capitalized on the AI boom as a Southeast Asian logistics hub that packages and re-exports semiconductors from neighboring countries.
③ Relative Decline of Traditional Manufacturing Powers Japan and Germany
Manufacturing powers outside the AI supply chain or reliant on traditional industries struggled. Japan, which fell to 9th place with a 6.5% export growth rate in the first half, is a prime example. While some sectors like semiconductor manufacturing equipment performed well, its largest export—automobiles—was hampered by U.S. tariff barriers and sluggish demand in China. Structural factors, such as Japan’s overseas production share rising from 11.8% in 2000 to 25.3% in 2024, further reduced domestic export statistics. Germany, the world’s 3rd-largest exporter, also lagged behind South Korea and Taiwan with a mere 10.8% export growth rate in the first half. Affected by low-cost competition from Chinese electric vehicles, Germany’s automotive exports fell 10.6% from January to June.
Park Min-jun, head of KOTRA’s Trade and Investment Research Center, said, “To solidify South Korea’s position as a top-five exporter and achieve the 1 trillion dollar milestone, the country must diversify its export engines into bio, defense, and consumer goods, leveraging its ultra-competitive semiconductor sector as a fulcrum.”

articles.title: U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan Semiconductor Dominance Faces Chinese Challenge - 조선일보
articles.summary: U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan Semiconductor Dominance Faces Chinese Challenge  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Apple, a U.S. tech giant, is a major player in the global semiconductor market. Its iPhones and MacBooks are equipped with memory chips like DRAM and NAND flash, as well as in-house developed application processors (APs). Last year, Apple procured over 19 billion chips from U.S. supply chains, mostly from South Korean, U.S., and Taiwanese companies.
Recently, Apple has been considering the use of DRAM from Chinese ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). John Ternus, Apple’s chief operating officer, stated on the 15th, “We must review all options, including Chinese-made memory.” While actual adoption remains uncertain due to U.S. regulations and political opposition, Apple’s shift reflects the changing realities of the semiconductor industry.
The global semiconductor industry has long been led by the U.S. in technology and standards, with South Korea and Taiwan supporting manufacturing in memory and foundry sectors, respectively. However, China is now disrupting this structure by leveraging massive capital, strong government policies, and a vast domestic market to rapidly advance its production and technological capabilities.
Some analysts predict that by 2030, China will become the world’s largest semiconductor producer. Concerns are growing that the global semiconductor dominance long held by South Korea, the U.S., and Taiwan could shift to China, starting with memory chips. Chris Miller, a professor at Tufts University, wrote in his book *Chip War*, “Semiconductors have shaped the structure of international politics, the global economy, and the balance of military power.”
◇Industry Built by the U.S., Division of Labor with Korea and Taiwan
Semiconductors are essential components for products requiring information processing, from computers and smartphones to home appliances, automobiles, and toys. A single smartphone contains dozens of chips, while a car can have up to 3,000, from engine control units to headlights. Artificial intelligence (AI), a cornerstone of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, also relies on semiconductors.
The modern semiconductor industry began in the U.S. with the invention of the transistor in 1947. Fairchild Semiconductor, founded in 1957, laid the foundation for mass production of integrated circuits (ICs), and Intel, established in 1968, ushered in the era of CPUs and DRAM in the 1970s. Companies like Intel and Texas Instruments led the integrated semiconductor industry, handling design, production, and packaging.
In the 1980s, Japan challenged U.S. dominance by leveraging its manufacturing base and large-scale investments to dominate the memory market. By 1986, Japan became the world’s largest semiconductor supplier, with an 80% share of the DRAM market the following year. Facing this pressure, the U.S. signed the U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement in September 1986, which included measures to curb Japan’s dominance. A surging yen eroded Japan’s price competitiveness, and missed investment opportunities led to its decline.
South Korea and Taiwan filled the gap. Samsung Electronics developed 64K DRAM in 1983 and became the world’s top DRAM producer in 1992 by releasing the first 64M DRAM, overtaking Japan. Taiwan took a different path: Morris Chang, a former TI executive, founded TSMC in 1987 with government support, establishing the foundry model.
The semiconductor industry then split into fabless design, foundry, and integrated device manufacturing, forming a global division of labor. U.S. fabless companies like NVIDIA, AMD, and Qualcomm focused on design, accelerating advancements in GPUs for AI and other semiconductors.
◇China Challenges Semiconductor Hegemony with Capital and Domestic Market
China, once a peripheral player, is now challenging the U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan semiconductor alliance. Starting with the founding of foundry SMIC in 2000, China entered the memory market in 2016 by establishing CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), recruiting talent from Korean firms.
Its production expansion, fueled by government subsidies and domestic demand, is remarkable. CXMT’s monthly DRAM wafer production capacity is estimated to grow from 20,000 wafers in 2019 to about 350,000 by the end of this year—a 17.5-fold increase. This nears Samsung’s capacity (about 720,000 wafers) and approaches U.S. Micron’s (about 385,000 wafers).
Technological progress is also alarming. Huawei released the Ascend AI accelerator to rival NVIDIA, and CXMT announced plans to launch next-generation server DRAM before Samsung and SK Hynix. Counterpoint Research noted, “U.S. export restrictions have paradoxically accelerated China’s semiconductor development, giving it a chance to catch up.”
The European Court of Auditors (ECA) projected that China’s share of global semiconductor production capacity will rise from 11% in 2010 to 22% by 2030, becoming the largest producer. A high-ranking official from the domestic industry said, “China’s semiconductor growth is already a major threat to the Korean economy. We must widen the gap in HBM, next-generation DRAM, and NAND.”

articles.title: Axcelis Breaks Ground in Pyeongtaek: Ion Implant Maker Bets $35M on Korea Chip Supercycle - Tech Times
articles.summary: Axcelis Breaks Ground in Pyeongtaek: Ion Implant Maker Bets $35M on Korea Chip Supercycle  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
A Beverly, Massachusetts equipment maker is planting its manufacturing operations in the center of the most aggressive semiconductor capacity buildout the world has seen, breaking ground today on a $35 million ion implantation facility in Pyeongtaek, South Korea — the same city where Samsung Electronics is simultaneously constructing what may become the largest semiconductor factory complex ever built under a single campus.
Axcelis Technologies (Nasdaq: ACLS), whose Purion family of ion implanters equips chipmakers from Beverly to Busan, is beginning construction on a 200,000-square-foot (approximately 18,580 square meters) manufacturing center in Pyeongtaek's Gyeonggi Province. The facility is designed to handle the full manufacturing lifecycle of ion implantation equipment — including Class 1,000 and Class 10,000 cleanrooms, warehousing, and a dedicated customer training center — with production targeted for the second half of 2028.
The timing and the address are not accidental. Ion implanters are indispensable tools in front-end semiconductor fabrication, and Pyeongtaek is now one of the most consequential postal codes in global chipmaking.
Why Pyeongtaek, Why Now
Directly adjacent to where Axcelis is building, Samsung Electronics is advancing construction of its P5 campus — a facility that, under an amendment to raise its floor area ratio from 350% to 490%, is being redesigned from a dual-fab to a triple-fab structure, accommodating up to six cleanrooms, per an approved amendment. According to TrendForce, P5-1 and P5-2 combined are expected to form the world's largest semiconductor manufacturing facility by individual fab scale, with P5-1 exterior construction now complete and production targeting late 2028.
Neighboring Yongin, a 30-minute drive away, tells a comparable story. SK hynix's board approved $38.3 billion (approximately 54.3 trillion won) in new fab investments in August 2026, covering its Y2 DRAM facility at the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster and a NAND flash plant in Cheongju. The Y2 facility will be the second of four fabs planned for the Yongin cluster, with its first Y2 cleanroom opening expected in June 2029. SK hynix has already accelerated its four-fab Yongin timeline from 2045 to 2033 completion.
The scale of investment in this corridor is hard to overstate. In late June 2026, Samsung and SK hynix jointly announced a combined 800 trillion won investment — approximately $600 billion at current exchange rates (approximately $518 billion at the announcement-day rate of roughly 1,547 won per dollar) — earmarked for four new fabs in South Korea. The Korean government's stated goal is to double national DRAM production capacity within five years.
For a supplier of ion implanters, a local manufacturing hub inside that ecosystem is not a market-development initiative. It is a bid for near-term tool orders and the aftermarket revenue that follows wherever those tools are qualified.
What Ion Implanters Actually Do
Ion implantation is the step in semiconductor fabrication where a beam of electrically charged atoms — ions — is fired into a silicon wafer to precisely alter its electrical properties, creating the transistor junctions and doping profiles that determine how a chip behaves. Every modern logic and memory device requires between 20 and 80 or more implant steps per wafer at advanced nodes, making ion implanters among the highest-demand tools in a fab's equipment fleet. Advanced DRAM wafers may require even more, as scaling pushes toward higher layer counts and tighter tolerances.
The process requires three functional components: an ion source (where a dopant gas such as phosphine, boron trifluoride, or arsenic trifluoride is ionized in a plasma chamber), an accelerator (which drives the ions to precise energies before they enter the wafer), and a target chamber (where the beam is scanned across the wafer surface with micron-level uniformity). Ion energies typically range from 10 kiloelectronvolts (keV) for shallow surface implants to several megaelectronvolts (MeV) for deep retrograde-well implants in CMOS logic — a range spanning six orders of magnitude that a single fab may need to cover across its full process flow.
Axcelis vs. Applied Materials: The Architecture That Sets the Stakes
Axcelis holds approximately 40% of the global ion implanter market, making it the primary commercial alternative to Applied Materials' VIISta product line. The competitive distinction between them runs deeper than market position: it lives in how the two companies have organized their product architectures.
Applied Materials operates multiple specialized VIISta product lines, each optimized for a specific implant class — high current, high energy, medium current — requiring customers to manage separate qualification processes, spare-parts inventories, and operator training protocols for each platform. Axcelis built its entire Purion family on a single unified chassis, from the Purion M medium-current system to the Purion XEmax high-energy platform, which uses a dual LINAC (radio-frequency linear accelerator) design with patented Boost Technology to deliver energies up to 15 MeV. The 12-stage LINAC design in the standard Purion XE reaches 4.5 MeV, while the XEmax dual-LINAC configuration reaches 15 MeV — energies required for the deepest well-formation implants in advanced DRAM and next-generation power management chips.
The RF LINAC approach offers a specific advantage for purity: the Purion XEmax's dual LINAC design removes metal and particulate contamination at levels other designs cannot match, an attribute that matters enormously at memory fabs where a single contaminated lot can cost millions of dollars in yield loss.
The unified-chassis strategy has proven particularly effective at memory fabs running high volume across multiple implant classes simultaneously. At a Samsung or SK hynix facility running dozens of process modules, a single-platform supplier simplifies process qualification, reduces spare-parts complexity, and lowers operator retraining costs every time a new device generation is introduced.
The switching-cost dynamics are equally significant: re-qualifying a competitor's implant system into a production flow typically requires weeks to months of engineering effort, reduced fab throughput during the qualification period, and meaningful yield risk at the start of production. Customers who qualify Purion systems into a leading-edge flow have a strong economic incentive to extend that qualification — and therefore to continue buying from Axcelis — into subsequent nodes.
The Facility Itself
The Pyeongtaek site will span approximately 200,000 square feet (about 18,580 square meters) of total gross floor area and is designed around what Axcelis describes as a "lean production environment" incorporating nearly 50 years of semiconductor capital equipment experience. The cleanroom classifications — Class 1,000 and Class 10,000, corresponding to ISO Class 6 and ISO Class 7 — are the same contamination-controlled environments found inside the chip fabs Axcelis equips, allowing the company to assemble, test, and calibrate implanters in conditions that match their eventual operating environment.
The customer training center is a strategically notable element. Ion implanters are process-sensitive tools that require significant application engineering before they can be qualified for high-volume production at a customer site. Having that capability physically embedded in South Korea — rather than routing it through Beverly, Massachusetts — reduces the time and logistical friction between tool delivery and production-qualified operation, which matters when a fab's ramp timeline is measured in quarters.
The investment was announced September 8, 2026, accompanied by a formal Investment Declaration Ceremony in Washington, D.C., where Axcelis Executive Vice President of Global Operations Robert Mahoney participated alongside officials from South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources (MOTIR) and the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA). The ceremony included representatives of four American companies committing a combined $2 billion across semiconductors, advanced materials, and energy in South Korea.
The Business Case in Numbers
Axcelis's recent financials frame why this investment is happening now. The company reported Q2 2026 revenue of $215.2 million, exceeding analyst estimates, and raised its full-year 2026 guidance to year-over-year revenue growth — an upgrade from the earlier flat-growth projection, driven by recovering memory demand and strength in power-device markets. For Q3 2026, Axcelis guided revenue of approximately $230 million, with non-GAAP earnings per diluted share of approximately $1.11. The company enters this capital commitment from a position of financial strength, with $557 million in cash and securities at the close of fiscal 2025 and $107 million in free cash flow generated that year despite lower revenues.
Ion implantation accounted for 98.2% of Axcelis's fiscal 2025 revenue of $839 million, making the Korea market more than a growth option — it is a direct lever on the company's core business. For context, full-year 2024 revenue was approximately $1.02 billion before the memory-market correction reduced spending in the back half of the year; the recovery now in progress, driven by DRAM and HBM demand from AI workloads, represents the business environment in which this facility is being built.

USD/JPY Forecast: Mizuho Sees Gradual Dollar-Yen Decline
Mizuho sees scope for the Japanese Yen to strengthen against the US Dollar, but expects easing inflation to limit the Bank of Japan's rate rises.
The Japanese Yen edged higher on Wednesday, taking the US Dollar-to-Yen exchange rate to 158.08, down 0.13% on the day.
Mizuho sees scope for USD/JPY to decline gradually, although its argument relies partly on lower US yields rather than an extended series of Japanese interest-rate increases.
The bank expects the BoJ to pause in October and raise rates in December, then slow the pace of tightening in 2027 as energy inflation subsides and pressure on the Yen eases.
Its assessment, based on information available on 16 October, questions how far markets expect Japanese borrowing costs eventually to rise.
That adds a qualification to the Yen recovery forecasts from Westpac and Goldman Sachs examined on Tuesday: a stronger currency need not depend on increasingly aggressive BoJ tightening.
December hike remains in view
Mizuho forecasts the overnight call-rate target at 1.50% at end-2026 and 1.75% by June 2027, remaining at that level through September.
That would mean two further quarter-point increases from the 1.25% rate set by the BoJ in September.
Chief bond strategist Noriatsu Tanji and market analyst Yuhi Kawano identify lingering pressure from imports:
"Given the rise in crude oil prices due to the escalation of tensions in Iran, inflation is likely to accelerate to some extent in 2H 2026 given the existence of items affected with a lag (such as electricity prices), various spillover effects, and the impact of the YoY decline in the yen."
"With the BOJ increasingly worried about weakness in the yen, we expect rate hikes to continue at three-month intervals through the end of 2026."
"Thereafter, we project the Bank will resume hiking once every six months, in part because lower US rates (following a Fed decision to forgo further hikes) are likely to ease downward pressure on the yen."
Mizuho does not need the Fed to start cutting rates for that argument to work: an end to US tightening could allow market yields to fall and reduce the Dollar's attraction relative to the Yen.
Its analysts also doubt that domestic inflation will justify the eventual policy rate investors have anticipated.
"And with underlying inflation in Japan struggling to gain traction and the policy rate already within the BOJ's estimated neutral range, the hurdles to further hikes are likely to rise starting in 2H 2027, when energy inflation subsides."
"We believe the terminal rate of 2% or more currently being priced in is excessive and expect yields to begin declining in 2027 as these expectations fade."
The terminal rate is the expected peak of the tightening cycle, rather than the rate at the next meeting.
Why falling bond yields can accompany Yen gains
Mizuho's currency view also draws on the reversal in US government-bond yields after the inflation release last week.
Treasury yields initially rose, then fell as equities weakened, and remained subdued even when shares recovered.
The analysts write: "Moreover, rates fell even as expectations for an October rate hike rose slightly following the upside surprise in the US CPI the day before."
"Taken together, these developments may indicate that the somewhat excessive-looking, term-premia-driven rise in long-term US rates since August has begun to unwind."
The term premium is the extra return investors require for holding longer-dated debt rather than repeatedly buying short-term securities.
A decline in that premium can pull bond yields lower without a corresponding reduction in the central bank's policy rate.
Mizuho connects that shift to the Yen: "We think this reversal, together with the gradual decline in USD/JPY that it may have prompted, will be supportive of JGBs."
JGBs are Japanese government bonds, whose prices rise when their yields fall.
The bank forecasts the 10-year JGB yield declining from 2.90% at end-2026 to 2.40% by September 2027, even as its projected overnight policy rate rises.
It nevertheless expects uncertainty over Japanese fiscal policy and government borrowing to limit the near-term fall in bond yields.
Its US inflation assumption remains vulnerable, however:
"Our baseline scenario assumes the pick-up in US inflation caused by the war in Iran will prove temporary, allowing the Fed to discontinue rate hikes next year."
More persistent inflation could prolong US tightening and renew downward pressure on the Yen.
Mizuho identifies that as a risk which could also force Japan to raise rates more frequently than in its base case.
What This Means for USD/JPY
Mizuho's analysis supports gradual Yen appreciation without supplying a numerical USD/JPY target. Lower US yields would help that recovery, while a reassessment of how far Japanese rates can rise could temper the support available from domestic policy.
Japan's September inflation figures, due on 23 October, will test whether price pressures are becoming more persistent. Evidence of persistent underlying inflation would challenge Mizuho's expectation that the obstacles to further tightening will increase next year.
The BoJ's 29-30 October meeting and updated outlook will then test its expectation of an October pause. An unchanged rate accompanied by preparations for December would fit Mizuho's view, while evidence that policymakers see a more lasting inflation problem would make its limited tightening path harder to sustain.

articles.title: Japan is Just “Months” Away From Running Out of a Critical Rare Earth Mineral. Here’s Why Rare Earths are Becoming AI’s Biggest Bottleneck. - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.summary: Japan is Just “Months” Away From Running Out of a Critical Rare Earth Mineral. Here’s Why Rare Earths are Becoming AI’s Biggest Bottleneck.  24/7 Wall St.
articles.full_text:
China controls most of the world's yttrium supply, Japan says it has months left, and the US has no commercial plant to fill the gap. Three American rare earth stocks barely reacted, and the reason reveals a deeper vulnerability in…
Japan has told Washington it is “months” from running out of yttrium, a rare earth used in jet engines and chipmaking equipment, and has asked the US to help push China to ease its export restrictions. The Financial Times reported the warning first on October 20, 2026. Kalshi posted on X on October 20, 2026: “JUST IN: Japan says it is “months” from running out of yttrium and asks the US to help push China to ease rare earth curbs”. On October 21, China defended its restrictions on Japan and cited concerns about Japanese “remilitarization.”
US rare earth stocks barely moved. In early trading on October 21, MP Materials (NYSE:MP) rose 1.11% to $39.48. USA Rare Earth (NASDAQ:USAR) gained 1.29% to $10.19, and Energy Fuels (NYSEAMERICAN:UUUU) added 2.13% to $8.39. Over the past month, the three had fallen 16.46%, 33.7% and 28.29%.
What Japan’s Warning Actually Covers
So far, Japan has only described a shortage and made a request. No US commitment, deal or timeline has been announced.
Yttrium goes into heat-resistant coatings on jet-engine parts, into electronics, and into semiconductor manufacturing equipment, so it feeds directly into the AI chip expansion. The US Geological Survey estimates that 2025 global mine production was 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes of yttrium oxide equivalent, and China produced most of it. The US has no fully commercial plant to separate yttrium (split mixed ore into individual elements) or refine it (purify it to usable grade). US yttrium oxide imports fell to zero in May and June 2026. Reuters then reported that 29 tonnes more were approved for July.
China has done this before. It restricted shipments to Japan in 2010, tightened its restrictions in early 2026 and stopped key exports to Japan in July 2026. The US and China discussed a truce in May 2026, but the restrictions kept biting.
Which Stocks Are Impacted
MP Materials: It runs the Mountain Pass mine and sells NdPr oxide and metal (the main magnet feedstock) plus gadolinium. It also makes magnets in Fort Worth. Second-quarter revenue rose 89% to $108.49 million. Its first heavy rare earth separation circuit remains on track to produce terbium and dysprosium later this year. Management has called yttrium only a potential opportunity. MP has announced no yttrium revenue.
USA Rare Earth: This is the speculative name. Second-quarter revenue was $5.82 million, missing expectations. It owns the Round Top heavy rare earth deposit in Texas, a magnet plant in Stillwater, Oklahoma, and Less Common Metals in the UK. It is also buying Serra Verde for about $2.8 billion. We could not verify any yttrium production.
Energy Fuels: It is mainly a uranium miner. Its White Mesa Mill in Utah produces NdPr oxide and has made high-purity terbium and dysprosium. We could not verify any yttrium production.
Why the Market Shrugged
All three companies are built around magnets, and MP’s chief executive said in August that “the vast majority of demand is no-heavy.” A yttrium shortage hits Japanese aerospace and chip-tool supply chains before it reaches US magnet economics.
The long-term demand case is stronger. Magnets power the motors and actuators in humanoid robots and EVs, as well as data center cooling and power equipment (the same picks-and-shovels angle behind the AI expansion we mapped in a free report on seven suppliers powering AI infrastructure). He added that “30 million or 40 million humanoid robots a year” would use up “100% of rare earth magnet production globally, including China.” New supply from African and friendly projects, however, takes years to reach production and pass customer approval. A shortage measured in months will not wait for it.
Does Japan’s Yttrium Crunch Change the Case for These Stocks?
Not in the near term. The warning shows how much power China holds, but it adds no revenue to any of these three companies. MP remains the only one with revenue at scale and a working heavy rare earth circuit. USA Rare Earth stays a development-stage story.
There are four milestones to watch. First, whether China eases its restrictions on Japan before year-end. Second, whether US yttrium oxide imports resume beyond the 29 tonnes Reuters reported for July. Third, whether MP reports its first dysprosium and terbium output by December 31, 2026. Fourth, whether USA Rare Earth reaches 600 MTPA run-rate capacity at Stillwater in Q4 2026.

The South Korean government and 24 companies and institutions, including Hyundai Motor, have formed a "one team" partnership to target the fast-growing automotive semiconductor market driven by the spread of electric and self-driving vehicles. The strategy is to cooperate across the entire cycle, from design to production and in-vehicle validation, to build a mass-production track record for domestic chips and fundamentally reshape a supply chain dominated by foreign products. Hyundai Mobis in particular aims to apply nine automotive semiconductors now under development with local partners to mass-produced Hyundai Motor and Kia vehicles in 2029.
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said on the 21st that a one-team task force involving Hyundai Motor, Hyundai Mobis and LG Electronics was launched at a special session of the 2026 Automotive Semiconductor Korea forum held in Pangyo, Gyeonggi Province. Under the structure, automakers and parts suppliers present the specifications they need, fabless firms handle the design, and foundry and packaging companies manufacture the chips. The ministry plans to identify joint projects and link them to support for research and development, infrastructure and workforce training.
Automotive semiconductors control power from engines, motors and batteries, process driving data for advanced driver assistance systems, and support in-vehicle communications and infotainment. With demand rising as electric and self-driving vehicles spread, the global market is projected to grow to $133 billion (about 176 trillion won) by 2030 from $77.4 billion last year.
Yet South Korea, a powerhouse in memory chips, has little presence in automotive semiconductors. According to the government, the local content ratio for automotive chips was about 5% last year, with a global market share of just 3%. Industry officials have called for a cooperation model that brings automakers, parts suppliers, fabless firms and foundries together from the earliest stage of development, along with a larger R&D budget and support for performance testing, certification and field demonstration.
At the forum, Hyundai Mobis also signed a memorandum of understanding with SK keyfoundry, four small and midsize fabless companies and four support organizations to build a process and evaluation ecosystem for automotive power semiconductors. The company will set up a dedicated R&D facility for developing silicon carbide power semiconductors for vehicles, and a comprehensive semiconductor support center in Cheonan will begin full operation in June next year.
Hyundai Mobis has already begun developing 13 automotive semiconductors in partnership with domestic companies, and for nine of them it has selected target vehicle models in consultation with Hyundai Motor and Kia.
Lee Kyu-seok, president of Hyundai Mobis, told a press briefing that day that the chips would be installed in vehicles launching as early as 2029. He added that controllers equipped with the semiconductors would be put into early vehicle testing starting next year.

articles.title: TSMC Kumamoto 3nm Fab Approved, but Japan Is Trading Volume for Advanced Chips - remio
articles.summary: TSMC Kumamoto 3nm Fab Approved, but Japan Is Trading Volume for Advanced Chips  remio
articles.full_text:
TSMC secured Japanese approval for its TSMC Kumamoto 3nm fab, targeting 6,000 300-millimeter wafers per month by late 2028. The decision gives Japan its first planned domestic manufacturing capacity for 3nm logic chips. It also replaces a much larger factory plan centered on older processes.
That exchange creates the real story. Japan is not simply gaining another semiconductor plant. It is trading tens of thousands of planned monthly wafers for a smaller pool of more valuable, technically demanding production.
TSMC says strong demand linked to artificial intelligence drove the change. Yet 6,000 wafers represent a modest starting capacity beside the company’s broader expansion in Taiwan and Arizona. The factory must still install complex equipment, recruit qualified workers, transfer processes, and reach competitive yields before the approval becomes dependable supply.
Japan’s other advanced-chip project adds another point of tension. Rapidus wants to begin producing 2nm chips in Hokkaido, while TSMC will bring its established 3nm process to Kumamoto. One project seeks to create a domestic foundry champion, while the other imports the manufacturing system of the global market leader.
The approval therefore marks a strategic shift, not a finished victory. It gives Japan a credible path into advanced logic manufacturing, but the factory’s scale and execution will decide how much that path changes the market.
Japan Approved a Different Factory, Not Just a New Process
The revised plan turns Kumamoto’s second factory from a high-volume site for established nodes into a smaller advanced-logic operation.
Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry approved the amended production plan on October 16, 2026. The applicant is Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing, or JASM, TSMC’s majority-owned Japanese manufacturing subsidiary.
Under the approved plan, JASM intends to produce 3nm logic semiconductors at the second Kumamoto factory. A process node identifies a generation of chip-manufacturing technology, although the nanometer label no longer describes one physical feature precisely.
The project lists planned capacity of 6,000 wafers per month, measured as 300-millimeter equivalents. Initial shipments are scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2028, with production expected to continue for at least ten years.
Those details differ sharply from the original plan approved in 2024. That version centered on 12nm and 6nm logic chips, with additional 40nm capacity tied to domestic demand. Its principal 12nm and 6nm lines were designed for 48,000 wafers per month.
The wider second-factory plan had reached 63,000 wafers per month when the additional 40nm output was included. The revised project concentrates on 3nm production at less than one-tenth of that headline wafer volume.
This does not mean Japan is losing nine-tenths of the factory’s economic value. Advanced chips require more processing steps, more expensive equipment, and tighter production control. A wafer carrying 3nm processors can also support products with much higher computing value than many mature-node components.
However, wafer capacity still matters. Six thousand wafers offer less room for customer diversification, production interruptions, and uneven early yields. The number describes nominal input capacity, not the quantity of usable chips shipped to customers.
The revised production plan also identifies customers in Japan as the main intended recipients. That provision connects public support to domestic supply security rather than treating the plant as another unrestricted export base.
The approved investment scope is listed at $10.8 billion, down from $12.2 billion in the earlier certified plan. Japan’s maximum subsidy commitment also falls from ¥732 billion to ¥645.15 billion under the revision.
Those figures do not settle the factory’s eventual size. Additional investment or production phases could still change its economics, but those possibilities are not part of the currently approved 6,000-wafer plan.
Japan’s action provides regulatory and subsidy certainty for the new direction. It does not certify future yield, customer orders, or an effortless technology transfer. Those operational tests begin long after the paperwork ends.
The first Kumamoto factory also received a revised plan. Its projected capacity moved from 55,000 to 50,000 monthly wafers, with production focused on 22nm, 28nm, and 40nm processes.
Together, the changes give the two neighboring factories clearer roles. The first serves established automotive, industrial, and image-sensor demand. The second becomes Japan’s foothold in advanced computing silicon.
That division creates a more specialized manufacturing cluster. It also abandons the original idea that the second factory would mainly extend the first plant’s higher-volume process range.
Why AI Demand Rewrote the TSMC Japan 3nm Plan
TSMC is redirecting Kumamoto because advanced AI computing has made 3nm capacity more valuable than the factory’s original mix.
TSMC disclosed the intended upgrade in February 2026, months before Japan formally approved it. Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei presented the proposal during a meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
The company linked the decision to demand for AI-related computing. Three-nanometer processes are suited to large processors that need high transistor density, strong performance, and controlled power consumption.
That does not mean every 3nm wafer becomes an AI accelerator. The same process family can serve smartphone processors, central processing units, networking chips, and custom application-specific integrated circuits.
AI demand still changes the investment calculation. Cloud providers and chip designers are commissioning increasingly complex processors, while leading-edge foundry capacity remains concentrated among very few manufacturers.
TSMC had previously positioned Kumamoto around automotive, industrial, consumer, and high-performance computing demand. Its original factory plan described two factories exceeding 100,000 monthly wafers across several process generations.
The new direction narrows that mix. Instead of spreading the second facility across mature and advanced-but-established nodes, TSMC is assigning it one of the company’s major current process families.
This forms part of a larger 3nm expansion rather than a standalone Japanese bet. TSMC is adding advanced capacity in Tainan and Arizona while converting some 5nm tools in Taiwan to support 3nm production.
During its October earnings call, TSMC said it was adding three new 3nm fabs across Taiwan, Arizona, and Japan. The company described a multiyear demand pipeline and reiterated that Kumamoto volume production remains scheduled for 2028.
The earnings call transcript places Japan within a coordinated global capacity plan. It does not present Kumamoto as a replacement for Taiwan, which remains TSMC’s research and manufacturing center.
Timing also explains the choice. TSMC’s 3nm technology is already an established commercial platform, rather than an experimental process awaiting its first customers.
The company reported that 3nm products generated 24 percent of its wafer revenue during 2025. That share demonstrates substantial market adoption, although revenue share does not reveal the capacity or yields planned for Japan.
Kumamoto is scheduled to start in 2028, several years after TSMC began producing 3nm chips in Taiwan. This delay gives the company time to transfer a more mature production system, including established process recipes and operating procedures.
The tradeoff is technological distance. By 2028, TSMC expects newer 2nm, N2P, A16, and A14 technologies to occupy the leading edge of its portfolio. Kumamoto’s 3nm line will be advanced, but it will not represent the company’s newest process.
That distinction matters for claims about national leadership. Japan will gain domestic advanced logic production, yet TSMC’s most advanced manufacturing and research will remain elsewhere.
The change also reflects the limits of planning a semiconductor factory years before production. Customers, products, and process economics can shift before construction and equipment installation finish.
A factory designed around 2024 demand assumptions risked opening with an outdated product mix. Revising the node now creates disruption, but it aligns the project with TSMC’s more recent assessment of customer demand.
Japan’s government supports the shift for a different reason. AI processors, robotics systems, and autonomous vehicles have become strategic technologies, making domestic access to advanced logic a national policy concern.
The economic security case received explicit support from Japan’s prime minister when TSMC announced the proposal. That political backing helps explain why regulators accepted such a substantial change to the subsidized project.
TSMC wants more globally distributed capacity for important customers. Japan wants domestic access to advanced chips and the manufacturing knowledge surrounding them. The revised factory sits where those interests overlap.
The TSMC Kumamoto 3nm Fab Trades Volume for Strategic Value
Kumamoto’s smaller output only makes sense if each wafer delivers greater strategic and commercial value than the displaced capacity.
Wafer counts cannot be compared without considering process complexity. A 3nm wafer passes through many demanding fabrication stages and can spend months inside the production system.
Advanced-node manufacturing also depends on extreme ultraviolet lithography, or EUV. EUV uses very short-wavelength light to print some of the smallest chip features onto silicon.

- Japan’s merchandise trade deficit came in at JPY 536.6 billion in September, far larger than the expected JPY 181.0 billion shortfall.
- USD/JPY traded around 158.30 in Asian dealings on Wednesday, with the pair maintaining a bullish technical bias above key moving averages.
- Japanese authorities highlighted close coordination between the government and the BoJ, while the Fed Chair kept a neutral tone on the next US rate decision.
Japan’s Trade Position Weakens as Growth in Flows Slows
USD/JPY advanced during Asian hours on Wednesday, trading near 158.30 after modest declines the previous day. The move came as the Japanese Yen (JPY) contended with fresh headwinds following the release of Japan’s latest merchandise Trade Balance figures from the Ministry of Finance.
Japan recorded a merchandise trade deficit of JPY 536.6 billion in September. While narrower than the JPY 1,111.9 billion shortfall in August, the figure substantially overshot expectations for a JPY 181.0 billion deficit and marked the fifth straight month of negative trade balance.
On a year-on-year basis, imports grew by 18.9%, easing from a 28.0% jump in August and coming in below the projected 19.6%. This was the slowest pace of import growth since May. Exports increased by 16.7% year-on-year, also missing estimates of 20.1% and marking their weakest growth rate in five months.
Despite the broader slowdown in import growth, crude oil imports surged 51.1%, reflecting Japan’s ongoing efforts to diversify its energy sources amid geopolitical uncertainties around the Strait of Hormuz.
Policy Coordination Emphasized by Japanese Authorities
On the policy front, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama stated on Wednesday that the government is working in close coordination with the Bank of Japan (BoJ). She stressed that there is no significant disagreement between fiscal authorities and the central bank concerning the inflation outlook or the stance of monetary policy.
Katayama acknowledged that tax reductions can stimulate demand and push prices higher, but underscored that the government intends to maintain a proactive and responsible fiscal approach. According to her comments, policy efforts will focus on enhancing Japan’s supply capacity while avoiding an acceleration in inflation.
US Inflation and Fed Signals in Focus
In the United States, recent data indicated that Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation accelerated in September. Market participants are now reassessing the Federal Reserve’s next steps following the latest remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
Chair Warsh stated that he does not “prejudge” interest rate decisions, offering no explicit guidance on whether policymakers will opt for another rate hike or keep policy unchanged at the upcoming October meeting.

On the daily chart, USD/JPY is trading at 158.30, sustaining a constructive near-term tone. The pair remains above both the nine-day and 50-day Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs), which continues to underpin the broader uptrend.
The 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI) is hovering around 54, signaling steady momentum that is not yet in overbought territory. This setup leaves room for buyers to extend the move higher. At the same time, the FXS Fed Sentiment Index reading of 127.51 points to a policy backdrop that remains supportive for the dollar.
On the downside, initial technical support is seen at the nine-day EMA at 158.20, followed by the 50-day EMA at 158.08. Together, these levels form a nearby demand band that reinforces the bullish structure. As long as USD/JPY trades above these moving averages on a closing basis, the technical bias favors further upside. A daily close below 158.08 would indicate waning momentum and could leave the pair vulnerable to a deeper corrective phase.

Buy. Korea’s semiconductor exports jumped +222.5% y/y, and Samsung is already re-rating as foreign investors return (+197.3bn won net). The market is shifting from “AI spend will slow” to “AI demand is real now,” and Samsung’s valuation (~3.5x forward earnings) is still below prior memory-cycle trough pessimism. Thesis: current memory pricing strength plus constrained supply keeps earnings resilient through the next cycle.
Key Risk: Memory prices fall faster than expected as supply ramps or AI/data-center capex gets delayed.
Buy. SK Hynix surged +7.11% alongside the export shock, and SK Securities raised 2027 profit forecasts as memory prices beat expectations. With Hynix typically more levered to memory pricing, the “cheap valuations” argument is strongest after the sell-off. Thesis: export receipts reflect durable demand and pricing power, not just a one-off spike.
Key Risk: A sharp reversal in memory pricing wipes out forecast earnings momentum.
- SK Hynix jumps 7.1% and Samsung gains 6.2% amid renewed foreign purchases.
- South Korea's chip exports surge 222.5% to $27.5bn in the first 20 days.
- Analysts see unusually cheap valuations despite strong AI memory demand.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares surged in Seoul on Wednesday after South Korea reported a 222.5% jump in semiconductor exports, providing fresh evidence of strong demand after a bruising sell-off in memory stocks.
SK Hynix jumped 7.11% to 1.31 million won, while Samsung climbed 5.56% to 223,250 won in morning trading. The KOSPI gained 3.28% by around 9:50 am, recovering part of Tuesday's 3.73% fall.
The figures exposed a growing gap between investors' concerns about future AI spending and the exceptional revenues chipmakers are generating today.
Samsung, SK Hynix stocks: Foreign buyers return
Foreign investors bought a net 197.3 billion won of Korean shares on Wednesday morning, reversing the selling that had weighed on the market. Institutions added 45.3 billion won, while retail investors sold 406.4 billion won.
The rebound followed improving sentiment towards US technology companies.
Super Micro Computer lifted its quarterly revenue forecast to $18.5 billion–$19.5 billion from $14.5 billion–$15.5 billion, reinforcing the view that demand for AI servers remains healthy.
Those signals helped investors reconsider last week's heavy selling, fuelled by concerns about rising borrowing costs and returns on data-centre investment.
Seo Sang-young of Mirae Asset Securities attributed the recovery to bargain hunting, stronger US semiconductor sentiment and more favourable overseas financial conditions.
He also cited expectations of lower oil prices, steadier long-term bond yields and a softer dollar.
Export figures challenge the bearish narrative
South Korea exported a record $27.5 billion of semiconductors during the first 20 days of October, up 222.5% from a year earlier, customs data showed.
Chips represented 44.7% of the country's $61.6 billion in total exports. Overall shipments by value rose 105.4%, while average daily exports, adjusted for working days, increased 65.9%.
The chip figure measures export value, not the number of units shipped. Higher memory prices can therefore lift revenues even without an equivalent rise in volumes.
The boom has also produced a striking split between financial markets.
“It is as if the stock market and the foreign exchange market are thinking differently,” Park Sang-hyun of iM Securities said, in comments translated by Chosunbiz.
He attributed the currency's resilience to semiconductor exports and the trade surplus, while equity investors were pricing in the possibility of slower AI investment.
Strong export receipts demonstrate current demand, but cannot guarantee that today's pricing strength will survive future changes in supply.
Cheap valuations put pessimism to the test
SK Securities analyst Han Dong-hee estimates Samsung trades at about 3.5 times forecast earnings over the next 12 months, compared with just 2.8 times for SK Hynix.
Those multiples have fallen below trough valuations seen in previous memory downturns, Han said in research on Wednesday.
He called expectations of a sharp earnings decline after 2028 “excessive pessimism”, citing AI demand, constrained supply and longer-term contracts.
SK Securities has raised its 2027 profit forecasts for both chipmakers as memory prices exceed expectations.
Still, forecasts could weaken quickly if data-centre projects stall, Chinese competitors expand or memory prices reverse.

Japan Nearing Wage-Driven Inflation Transition, Finance Minister Katayama Says
Japan's economy is experiencing price increases driven by higher import costs and is nearing a transition to a period of sustained inflation fueled by rising wages, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Wednesday, according to Reuters.
Katayama told parliament that the government's planned consumption tax cut and payouts are intended to soften the impact on households from rising living costs.
When asked by a lawmaker whether the government's tax cut plan could conflict with the central bank's efforts to fight inflation through interest rate increases, Katayama said the government and the Bank of Japan are exchanging views on various matters and that she sees no gap between their positions.
The Bank of Japan raised interest rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September, as an energy shock stemming from the Iran war, strong global demand related to artificial intelligence, and higher import costs from a weak yen increase the risk that underlying inflation will overshoot its 2% target.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration plans to cut by two years an 8% consumption tax rate on food items starting in April next year. Analysts have warned that the tax cut and the administration's large spending plans could boost demand and run counter to the central bank's efforts to contain inflation.
Katayama said it is true that tax cuts generally push up inflation by stimulating demand, but she added that the government will ensure its responsible and proactive fiscal policy boosts Japan's supply capacity in a way that does not accelerate inflation.

SEOUL/BEIJING/NEW YORK: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are upgrading their China factories to produce more advanced memory chips, four people familiar with the plans said, aiming to fend off competition from a fast-growing Chinese rival and meet huge AI demand.
How much to invest in their Chinese operations has become a tricky question for the South Korean semiconductor giants ever since the US began imposing export controls on some chip-making equipment in 2022 amid an effort to slow China's technological progress.
Both companies are now required to seek US licenses annually if they want to install US-made equipment such as etching machines in China. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security also said in 2025 it did not intend to grant licenses to upgrade technology and expand capacity at the foreign chipmakers' factories in China.
The regulatory headaches have limited their ability to refit their factories and contributed to loss of market share to Yangtze Memory Technologies Co (YMTC). Executives at the South Korean chipmakers have publicly warned that geopolitical tensions are undermining their Chinese operations.
Samsung confirmed in a statement to Reuters that upgrades were underway and were being done in close consultation with Washington. SK Hynix said it has been installing equipment at its Dalian factory in northeastern China, in consultation with the US government. Neither firm disclosed details of production plans that are being reported here for the first time.
Reuters could not, however, determine to what extent US authorities have granted export licences for equipment that Samsung and SK Hynix need for their planned upgrades.NAND memory chips with more than 200 layers at their Chinese plants, whose products are currently not as advanced as chips being produced in South Korea.
NAND, a type of memory chip that retains data without power, is widely used in smartphones, PCs and solid-state drives for AI data centres. More layers per chip means more storage density and lower costs.SAMSUNG SETS SIGHTS ON 286-LAYER CHIPS
As part of a project known internally as "Monami" - from the French for "my friend" - Samsung is converting the facility to make 286-layer V9 NAND chips, aiming for monthly output of 5,000 wafers in December this year and then a jump to 40,000 wafers by December 2027, one of the people said.
Samsung said its upgrade was in compliance with US export regulations, adding: "The upgrade is aimed at meeting growing demand from global customers, including those in the US. The company is not expanding production capacity or constructing new manufacturing facilities."
One of the people said the company is authorised to make chips with up to 240 layers at Dalian and may seek permission from Washington to conduct research and development on 300-plus-layer chips there that would help it lay the groundwork for potential production in the US.
