OTTAWA — As U.S. officials accuse Canada of interfering in American elections, Prime Minister Mark Carney says he spoke with U.S. President Donald Trump Wednesday morning, and added when asked specifically that they discussed “issues around trade.”
With the highly consequential U.S. midterm elections fast approaching and amid a protracted trade war between the two countries, Canada has yet to reach a new trade deal with the Americans.
“We discussed a wide range of things, wide range of issues, the situation in Iran,” Carney said.
“We talked a few days ago about Ukraine and those aspects there,” he added. “We talked about other aspects in the Middle East, and we did address some of the issues around trade.”
Carney made the remarks while taking questions from reporters on Parliament Hill Wednesday alongside Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
The two announced $9 billion in support for sectors affected by the trade war.
U.S. officials, meanwhile, released a fact sheet on Wednesday saying the government is monitoring Canadian activities in American politics. The sheet points to documents and appearances by Canadian officials — such as Industry Minister Melanie Joly, who is listed five four times — and claiming them as examples of interference.
Some of the examples include Joly saying Canada was targeting products that would most impact Republican states with its counter-tariffs, and the contentious Ontario anti-tariff ad campaign that cited former U.S. president Ronald Reagan.
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra issued a similar warning in a recent interview with “The Really Big Show” podcast, in which he warned Canadian politicians to stay out of American politics and said U.S. officials are monitoring potential “political interference in the U.S. midterms.”
The accusation comes just weeks after concerns in Canada about U.S. interference in Alberta’s referendum on Monday, which included a question on independence.
So-called separatist leader Jeffrey Rath said in an interview on CTV Question Period several months ago that he met with U.S. State Department officials.
And, earlier this month, the Globe and Mail published a sweeping investigation on key separatist leaders’ ties to Republican operatives in the United States.
In response to a question about the fact sheet on Wednesday, Carney said it was the U.S. that “initiated these trade actions.”
“We have responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, protect Canadian companies and to develop our economy,” he added.
Ford also responded to the question on Wednesday, saying: “I have no interest at all interfering in American elections.”
Trade war ongoing
After trade talks broke down in dramatic fashion in August, both countries slapped new tariffs on imports from the other. At the time, Trump and his administration lobbed a series of insults at Canada, posting several AI-generated memes online, and moved to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”
Then, in early September, Trump escalated U.S. trade actions against Canada, signing new executive orders to completely ban the import of certain Canadian products, including motorcycles and alcohol.
And, Trump last week said Canada will “end up being the 51st state,” a threat he’s now espoused for nearly two years.
“Canada treats us very badly,” he said during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz. “They always have. Not anymore. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town.”
Carney has previously said he speaks regularly with Trump, including in private calls and texts. He reiterated on Wednesday that Canada is “ready to sit down and negotiate” with the U.S. to hammer out a mutually beneficial deal.

articles.title: Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading Chinese factories to produce advanced RAM chips as AI data center competition ramps up — big players move to fight off the threat from CXMT and co. - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading Chinese factories to produce advanced RAM chips as AI data center competition ramps up — big players move to fight off the threat from CXMT and co.  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
The two biggest NAND flash memory manufacturers on the planet, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, are reportedly working to upgrade their Chinese factories to produce more advanced chips for use in AI data centers, Reuters reports. The move comes as the two companies continue to fight off competition from the fast-growing Chinese memory makers like CXMT. Fierce competition in the lucrative AI RAM market has already seen manufacturers slash consumer-focused production to allow them to increase production capacity for the more advanced — and money-spinning — components.
Citing four people familiar with the companies' plans, the report claims that Samsung Electronics aims to switch its Xian plant to the production of 286-layer flash chips by the end of the year. SK Hynix has its sights set a little lower, targeting chips with 240 or more layers at its Dalian facility. That factory was taken over back in 2021, but a timescale for the new upgrades isn't clear.
However, while Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are well placed to deal with the growing threat from Chinese chipmakers, both are faced with additional complications in the form of U.S. regulations. Export controls on chipmaking equipment were applied in 2022, with the aim of slowing China's technological progress. Both companies, based in South Korea, must now get licenses in order to install U.S.-built hardware in Chinese factories. The report points to this as a reason for the recent growth of Chinese firms like Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC). The company told investors at a recent IPO preparation meeting that it aims to become the world's largest NAND flash producer by the end of 2027.
While both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix say that they are working in consultation with the U.S. authorities, there's little doubt that this extra step has hampered the companies' ability to upgrade their factories to better meet the new AI memory demand.
It's impossible to overstate just how key Samsung and SK Hynix are to NAND supply. Samsung's Xian factory produces around 40% of the company's global output. It currently produces chips that have around 200 layers, but Samsung's plans aim to boost that to 286 layers for V9 NAND chips. For its part, SK Hynix's Dalian plant currently produces chips with 192 layers, with the company's aim for 240-layer chips reportedly confirmed by three people familiar with the plans.
Meanwhile, CXMT, China's premier chipmaker, is looking to move beyond DRAM production. A report from September 2026 noted that it was eyeing production of 3D NAND memory for use in solid-state storage (SSD) products. The country's largest DRAM producer, CXMT, posted $22.41 billion in revenue and $11.57 billion in net profit in the first half of 2026 after years of losing money. But despite this purple patch, the company is still much smaller than the likes of Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.

articles.title: Before they can vote, Korea’s teens are already swimming in election fraud content - Hankyoreh : English Edition
articles.summary: Before they can vote, Korea’s teens are already swimming in election fraud content  Hankyoreh : English Edition
articles.full_text:
A protester puts up a poster at the handball gymnasium in Olympic Park in Seoul’s Songpa District in June, during an ongoing protest to seal off the vote-counting center in Jamsil, sparked by a ballot paper shortage during the June 3 local elections. (Jung Yong-il/Hankyoreh)
          Editor’s note: For teenagers, Instagram is an all-purpose app. It serves as a messaging service for chatting with friends, a platform for watching videos, and a source of news and information about social issues and history. It can fairly be described as their window on the world.
Over the past year or two, however, a far-right worldview has begun to permeate that space. It is awash with hatred, mockery and fake news. The use of humor, memes and slick presentation makes it all the more dangerous.
While this is a new phenomenon in Korea, Instagram has long served as a gateway to the far right for teenagers and young adults in countries such as Germany and the US.
For this series of articles, the Hankyoreh conducted a data-driven analysis of the Instagram ecosystem.
 
On June 4, 2026, a post titled “Irrefutable evidence of election rigging in Tongyeong” appeared on the Instagram account “Ineugeum” (@dlsmrma, 23,000 followers).
Along with a screenshot of a news report about ballots being recounted for the mayoral election in Tongyeong, a city in South Gyeongsang Province, the post claimed that the decision had followed the discovery of 240 invalidated votes cast for a candidate from the conservative People Power Party.
But that was fake news. In the Tongyeong mayoral election, the candidate for the Democratic Party was elected by just 44 votes — the narrowest margin of Korea’s local elections on June 3. Election officials held two recounts to confirm the results. But while the margin narrowed to 38 votes, the outcome did not change.
Between June 3 and Sept. 15, a combined 755 posts claiming election fraud appeared on 48 major Instagram accounts studied by the Hankyoreh, or an average of seven posts per day. The posts collectively attracted 2.34 million Likes, based on 749 posts for which Like counts were publicly visible.
Claims of rigged elections stoked by certain far-right Instagram accounts spread like wildfire, even to teens. In a Hankyoreh survey of 604 people aged 14-18 last month, 46% said they saw or knew of posts alleging such fraud or phrases such as “Stop the Steal” within the past six months.
In addition, 28% said they agreed that the June local elections were “rigged and fraudulent.” Unlike other statements, such as “the martial law declaration was justified,” no major difference in opinion by gender was seen, with 28.5% of men and 27.5% of women agreeing with the sentiment.
The conspiracy theory that elections are rigged to favor a particular political party has become a staple of far-right populist discourse, undermining trust in the electoral system — a cornerstone of democracy. The narrative is spreading rapidly beyond unaffiliated voters to reach the next generation of voters.
Most survey respondents born between 2008 and 2012 will be eligible to vote in the next presidential election, in 2030.
Kindled by martial law, ignited by local elections 
An analysis of Naver DataLab search data for the term “election fraud” (bujeong seongeo) found that among Korean aged 13 to 18, search volume peaked during the presidential election last year and surged again right after the June elections this year, reaching 60% of the peak.
Shin Jin-wook, a professor of sociology at Chung-Ang University, called the trend troubling. 
“The election fraud narrative, which has spread even to teens following the insurrection attempt of December 2024, is dangerous because [as shown by the martial law declaration], it’s a conspiracy theory linked to the real-life subversion of the constitutional order,” he said. 
Through what chain of connections did the election fraud theory spread within the far-right ecosystem on Instagram? A Hankyoreh study examined two years’ worth of content — some 32,000 posts — from 48 big accounts that share far-right content, dividing such material into four groups by period.
              
              Hankyoreh graphic
          Based on major political developments, the four periods are: from the declaration of martial law to the impeachment ruling removing Yoon from office (December 2024-April 2025); his impeachment to last year’s presidential election (April-June 2025); the early days of the Lee administration (June 2025-May 2026); and after the June local elections (June 2026 onward). 
It was the fourth period examined that saw an explosive increase in posts backing an election fraud narrative. Leading the way were Ineugeum and “Politics Crush” (@politics_crush, 18,000 followers), a far-right YouTuber.
When related posts were grouped by posting date (within 72 hours) and similarity of content, the accounts that framed what was happening as election fraud the fastest were Ineugeum (10 times) and Politics Crush (8 times). Ineugeum in particular posted 101 of their election fraud posts — 47.2% of the 214 posts made over a two-year period — in the three months after the June 3 local elections.
During the fourth period examined, issues relating to election fraud and the National Election Commission accounted for 20% of all posts, second only to domestic politics (30%).
As election fraud claims spread rapidly through Instagram and other social media, they become a flashpoint inciting people who had previously been only loosely connected online into collective action. A prominent example can be seen in the 2021 attack on the Capitol in Washington, DC, by Donald Trump supporters. Many of the demonstrators at Olympic Park in Seoul’s Jamsil neighborhood reported participating after seeing news on Instagram or Threads.
The buildup to the explosion began shortly after the martial law declaration in December 2024.
Of the 48 accounts examined, the far-right YouTuber “Young Spirit” (@young.spirit_official, 39,000 followers) was the first to post an election fraud claim on Dec. 5, 2024, stating, “If election fraud comes to light, the Democratic Party should be disbanded.”
Two days later, another account called “Brother Bosu” (@brother_bosu, around 3,200 followers), which features content focusing chiefly on conservative politics, posted a video with the caption: “Why Yoon Suk-yeol stormed the National Election Commission.” Images in it showed ballots marked for Democratic Party candidates being counted by ballot sorters.
But the first period examined only showed a total of 50 posts alleging election fraud, or an average of 0.4 per day.
The second period began after Yoon’s impeachment and ran through the subsequent presidential election. During this time, the number of posts related to election fraud increased to 146, or 2.4 per day on average — suggesting the mobilization of such claims as a way of rallying conservatives ahead of the vote.
A full 101 of the posts made during this period came from the account “Youth Election Fraud Fighters” (@yeff_korea, 10,000 followers). Six other accounts, including Brother Bosu, began posting with hashtags such as “#electionfraud” and “#stopthesteal.” Since then, fraud claims have been trotted back out with each subsequent election.
Instagram ecosystem: From post-martial law seeds to a post-election forest
If the seeds of Instagram’s far-right ecosystem began sprouting around the time of the martial law declaration, they have flourished into a veritable forest since then by spreading election fraud claims.
Before the insurrection, the number of far-right figures operating Instagram accounts was small. It was an environment of scattered, separate activities by proponents of anti-feminist discourse — as exemplified by the group “New Man Power” — and far-right Protestants. With almost nothing connecting them, the situation was not one that could be described as an ecosystem.
After the martial law declaration, messages defending it began creating bridges between far-right Instagram accounts. As recently as September to November 2024, such accounts had not been using shared hashtags. By December, they were putting up posts with hashtags such as “#martiallaw” and “#electionfraud.”
              
              Hankyoreh graphic
          Brother Bosu and the far-right YouTube channel “Ground C” (@groundc.official, 53,000 followers) both began using the “#electionfraud” hashtag. Ahead of the Constitutional Court’s impeachment ruling, far-right YouTubers and young participants in anti-impeachment demonstrations united under the hashtag “#YoonAgain.” Before the presidential election, “#monitoringforelectionfraud” became their focus.
An examination of shared hashtags among the 48 accounts found just six pairs on average per month before April 2025 — compared with 76 in September of this year.
After the presidential election, the far-right ecosystem began expanding. This was the period when 26 of the 48 accounts — more than half — became active on Instagram.
A prime example can be found in the accounts associated with groups of younger people that were established in the wake of “Free University” (@freeuniv) and “Tantan Road” (@tantanroad.official), including “Mincho Board” (@mincho_board), “FLD” (@fld_4_ever) and “Houchin” (@houchin.official). Other accounts that began joining the ecosystem around this time included political factions like “Freedom and Innovation” (@freedominnovation) and far-right Christian ones like “Segero Church” (@segerochurch) and “The Monarch Report” (@monarchreport25). 
As the far-right Instagram ecosystem took shape, the issues explored within it diversified. By the third period examined — coinciding with the early part of the Lee Jae Myung presidency — defenses of the martial law declaration faded, as more and more users began criticizing the new administration’s policies or referring to relations with the US. articles.title: Nikkei 225 Rises 0.85% as Tokyo Stocks Recover From AI Jitters and Japan Exports Jump Nearly 17% in September - International Business Times Australia
articles.summary: Nikkei 225 Rises 0.85% as Tokyo Stocks Recover From AI Jitters and Japan Exports Jump Nearly 17% in September  International Business Times Australia
articles.full_text:
TOKYO — Japanese stocks rose on Wednesday, recovering some of their recent losses as technology shares advanced following a rally on Wall Street and as data showed a strong increase in Japan's exports.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 index closed up 545.82 points, or 0.85%, at 64,621.24.
The index opened at 64,885.95 and climbed to an intraday high of 65,404.63 in the first half-hour of trading, before giving back some of its gains to touch a low of 64,558.60 in the afternoon.
The gain followed two straight days of losses. On Tuesday, the Nikkei fell 1.30% to 64,075.37 as rising bond yields, inflation worries and doubts about AI financing weighed on the market, with SoftBank Group sliding 6%.
Exports surge
Investor sentiment was supported by trade data showing that Japan's exports jumped 16.7% in September from a year earlier, driven by strong sales of automobiles and computer-related components.
Imports rose even more sharply, climbing 18.9%, largely because of higher oil prices linked to the war involving Iran. That pushed Japan's trade deficit to nearly double from a year earlier.
Japan relies heavily on imported energy, making it particularly sensitive to oil price swings. Higher energy costs have added to inflation pressures and weighed on the trade balance.
Tech stocks recover
Japanese technology stocks advanced after a broad rally in U.S. shares overnight, driven by strong earnings from major American companies.
The gains mirrored a rebound in South Korea, where the KOSPI index surged more than 3% as chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rallied.
Technology and semiconductor-related stocks have been at the center of recent market volatility in Asia, as investors weigh the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and rising financing costs.
A turbulent October
The Nikkei has been volatile this month. On Oct. 15, the index plunged 4.9%, one of the largest one-day point drops in its history, before rebounding the following day.
Investors have been grappling with rising global bond yields, including higher U.S. Treasury yields, which have weighed on growth and technology stocks around the world.
Concerns about the financing of AI investments have also hit Japanese companies with heavy exposure to the sector, including SoftBank Group, a major investor in AI ventures.
Yen and policy outlook
Movements in the yen and expectations for Bank of Japan policy remain important drivers for Japanese stocks. A weaker yen tends to support exporters by boosting the value of overseas earnings, while rising interest rates in Japan could weigh on valuations.
Investors are also watching for signs of how inflation, driven partly by higher energy prices, could influence the central bank's next moves.
Strong year despite volatility
Despite recent swings, the Nikkei has posted significant gains over the past year, rising about 30%, supported by corporate governance reforms, strong earnings and foreign investment in Japanese equities.
What to watch
Investors will be watching upcoming corporate earnings, global bond yields, oil prices and developments in the technology sector for direction.
The performance of U.S. technology stocks and any further signs of stabilization in AI-related shares are also likely to influence Tokyo's market in the coming days.
